source_text: Sed ea satis erit praecerpsisse, in quibus et ratio Baptismi recognoscitur prima illa, qua jam tunc etiam ipso habitu praenotabatur ad Baptismi figuram, Dei spiritum, qui ab initio supervectabatur super aquas, intinctos reformaturum. Sanctum autem utique super sanctum ferebatur; aut ab eo quod superferebatur, id quod ferebat, sanctitatem mutuabatur. Quoniam subjecta quaeque materia, ejus quae desuper imminet, qualitatem rapiat necesse est, maxime corporalis spiritalem, et penetrare et insidere facilem per substantiae suae subtilitatem. Ita de Sancto sanctificata natura aquarum, et ipsa sanctificare concepit. Nemo dicat: Numquid ipsis enim aquis tinguimur quae tunc in primordio fuerunt? non utique ipsis nisi ex ea parte, qua genus quidem unum, species vero complures. Quod autem generi attributum est, etiam in specie redundat. Ideoque nulla distinctio est, mari quis an stagno, flumine an fonte, lacu an alveo diluatur, nec quidquam refert inter eos quos Joannes in Jordane, et quos Petrus in Tiberi tinxit. Nisi et ille spado, quem Philippus inter vias fortuita aqua tinxit, plus salutis aut minus retulit. Igitur omnes aquae de pristina originis praerogativa sacramentum sanctificationis consequuntur, invocato Deo. Supervenit enim statim spiritus de coelis, et aquis superest, sanctificans eas de semetipso, et ita sanctificatae vim sanctificandi combibunt. Quanquam ad simplicem actum competat similitudo, ut, quoniam vice sordium delictis inquinamur, aquis abluamur. Sed delicta, sicut non in carne comparent, quia nemo super cutem portat maculam idololatriae, aut stupri, aut fraudis; ita ejusmodi in spiritu sordent, qui est auctor delicti. Spiritus enim dominatur, caro famulatur; tamen utromque inter se communicant reatum, spiritus ob imperium, caro ob ministerium. Igitur medicatis quodammodo aquis per Angeli interventum, et spiritus in aquis corporaliter diluitur, et caro in eisdem spiritaliter mundatur.
pass_a_gloss: But it will be enough to have briefly mentioned those things, in which also the reason of Baptism is recognized, that first one, by which even then already by that very habit it was pre-noted for the figure of Baptism, the Spirit of God, who from the beginning was floating over the waters, was going to reform those who were dipped. But the Holy One was certainly carried over the holy one; or from that which was being carried over, that which was carrying, was borrowing holiness. Since every subject matter necessarily snatches the quality of that which looms over it from above, especially the spiritual over the bodily, and easily penetrates and settles in through the subtlety of its substance. Thus, from the Holy One, the nature of the waters was sanctified, and it itself began to sanctify. Let no one say: Are we indeed baptized in those very waters which were in the beginning? Not, of course, in those very ones, except in that part in which the genus is indeed one, but the species are several. But what has been attributed to the genus also overflows into the species. And therefore, there is no distinction, whether one is washed in the sea or in a pool, in a river or in a spring, in a lake or in a trough, nor does it matter among those whom John baptized in the Jordan, and those whom Peter baptized in the Tiber. Unless also that eunuch, whom Philip baptized with accidental water on the road, received more or less salvation. Therefore, all waters, by the prerogative of their original origin, attain the sacrament of sanctification, with God invoked. For the Spirit immediately comes from heaven, and remains over the waters, sanctifying them from Himself, and thus the sanctified waters will imbibe the power of sanctifying. Although the likeness is suitable for the simple act, so that, just as we are polluted by sins in the place of filth, we are washed with water. But sins, just as they do not appear in the flesh, because no one carries the stain of idolatry, or adultery, or fraud on his skin; so they pollute in the spirit, which is the author of sin. For the Spirit dominates, the flesh serves; yet both communicate the guilt between themselves, the Spirit on account of its command, the flesh on account of its ministry. Therefore, with the waters somehow medicated through the intervention of the Angel, and the Spirit is diluted bodily in the waters, and the flesh is spiritually cleansed in the same.

pass_b_english: That much will do for a quick survey of the points where the rationale of baptism first comes into view—points that even then were already flagged, by the very nature of the thing, as a foreshadowing of baptism: the Spirit of God, who from the beginning hovered over the waters, was going to remake those who would be dipped (Genesis 1:2). The Holy One was certainly borne above the holy element; or else the element that bore him borrowed its holiness from the One borne above. Since any underlying matter inevitably takes on the quality of what looms over it—especially when the spiritual overtakes the bodily, easily penetrating and settling in through the sheer subtlety of its substance—the nature of the waters was sanctified by the Holy One, and the waters themselves began to sanctify. No one should ask: 'Are we actually baptized in those very waters that existed at the beginning?' Of course not in those identical waters, except insofar as the genus is one while the species are many. What belongs to the genus overflows into the species as well. Therefore it makes no difference whether someone is washed in sea or pool, river or spring, lake or trough, nor does it matter between those John baptized in the Jordan and those Peter baptized in the Tiber—unless that eunuch whom Philip baptized with happenstance water on the road received more or less salvation. So all waters, by virtue of the prerogative of their original origin, obtain the sacrament of sanctification once God is invoked. For the Spirit comes at once from heaven and rests upon the waters, sanctifying them from himself, and thus the sanctified waters imbibe the power to sanctify. Admittedly a simple analogy fits the simple act: just as we are polluted by sins in place of filth, we are washed with water. But sins do not appear on the flesh, because no one carries the stain of idolatry, or sexual immorality, or fraud on his skin; rather they defile the spirit, which is the author of the sin. The Spirit commands, the flesh serves; yet both share the guilt between them—the Spirit because it commands, the flesh because it carries out the order. Therefore, with the waters in a sense medicated through the Angel's intervention, the Spirit is diluted bodily in the waters, and the flesh is cleansed spiritually in the same.

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source. The scripture citation (Genesis 1:2) added in Pass B is a correct identification of the allusion 'Dei spiritum, qui ab initio supervectabatur super aquas'.
